eras.name: Open frameworks
eras.text: Deep learning on GPUs for everyone
eras.background: Google trained its early deep networks on DistBelief, which used parameter servers on large clusters of CPU machines. Open-source frameworks then gave everyone automatic differentiation on GPUs. Deep models soon powered products such as YouTube's recommendations.

eras.name: Beyond one GPU
eras.background: Language models and recommenders both outgrew the memory of a single GPU. Language models split their layers across GPUs or sharded their training state. Recommenders sharded embedding tables too big for any one device.

eras.name: Memory-bound
eras.text: GPU memory traffic sets the pace
eras.background: Transformers became the most widely used architecture, and chat assistants made serving them a major cost. On GPUs, moving data through memory took longer than the arithmetic in most of their operations. Fused kernels, compilers and paged caches all attacked that memory traffic.

eras.name: Cluster scale
eras.background: A single training job came to fill a whole GPU cluster, where failures were routine. Serving split each request across pools of GPUs. Recommenders adopted the sequence models and scaling behavior of LLMs.

nodes.label: TensorFlow
nodes.problem: In Google's DistBelief, new layers meant C++ code and new optimizers meant changing its parameter servers.
nodes.idea: Express the model and its parameter updates as one dataflow graph, run anywhere from phones to GPU clusters.
nodes.impact: Google open-sourced it, and it became one of the most widely used deep learning frameworks.

nodes.label: YouTube DNN
nodes.problem: Factorization models used few signals, and scoring a huge video corpus for every request had to stay fast.
nodes.idea: A candidate network retrieves a short list by nearest-neighbor search, then a ranking network orders it.
nodes.impact: Deep models at every stage of the funnel became the norm in feeds, ads and search.

nodes.label: PyTorch
nodes.idea: Run each operation immediately as ordinary Python, recording it on the fly for automatic differentiation on GPUs.
nodes.impact: Researchers overwhelmingly preferred eager code, and graph frameworks, TensorFlow included, added eager modes.

from.why: Static graphs were built first and run later, which made models hard to write and debug.

nodes.label: Ring all-reduce
nodes.idea: GPUs average gradients by passing chunks to their neighbors in a ring, with no parameter server.
nodes.impact: Uber's Horovod and NVIDIA's NCCL spread it, and PyTorch's data-parallel training is built on it.

from.why: Its parameter servers clogged the network, and spreading a job over GPUs took heavy code changes.

nodes.label: ZeRO
nodes.idea: Shard optimizer state, gradients and weights across the data-parallel GPUs, fetching each piece only when needed.
nodes.impact: Microsoft shipped it in DeepSpeed, and PyTorch's fully sharded data parallelism grew from the same idea.

from.why: Every GPU held a full copy of weights and optimizer state, so big models ran out of memory.

nodes.label: DLRM
nodes.idea: Facebook shards embedding tables across devices with model parallelism and replicates the small dense layers.
nodes.impact: It became MLPerf's recommendation benchmark, a shared target for hardware and systems work.

from.why: Deep recommenders grew embedding tables far larger than one device, which frameworks could not shard.

nodes.label: Flash Attention
nodes.idea: FlashAttention computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory, fused into a single kernel.
nodes.impact: Long contexts became affordable, and PyTorch later shipped it as its built-in attention kernel.

from.why: Frameworks ran attention as separate operations, each writing a huge matrix out to slow GPU memory.

nodes.label: vLLM
nodes.problem: Serving engines reserved each request's KV cache for its longest possible answer, leaving most memory unused.
nodes.idea: PagedAttention stores the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like an operating system's memory pages.
nodes.impact: Larger batches cut serving cost, and vLLM became a leading open engine used by Meta and LinkedIn.

nodes.label: PyTorch 2
nodes.idea: TorchDynamo captures graphs from ordinary Python code, and TorchInductor compiles them into fused Triton kernels.
nodes.impact: Eager models could be compiled by adding one call, without rewriting them as graphs.

from.why: Each fused kernel like it was hand-written CUDA, and its authors called for compiling such kernels from PyTorch.

nodes.label: MegaScale
nodes.idea: ByteDance co-designs the model, parallelism and network, and automatically finds and evicts faulty machines.
nodes.impact: Made the case that fault tolerance and deep monitoring matter as much as parallelism at this scale.

from.why: Parallelism let one job span a whole cluster, where failures and slow nodes became constant.

nodes.label: DistServe
nodes.idea: DistServe runs the prompt (prefill) and decoding phases on separate GPUs, each with its own parallelism.
nodes.impact: Splitting the phases spread to DeepSeek's service and to open frameworks such as NVIDIA Dynamo and llm-d.

from.why: Prompt processing and token generation still shared GPUs, where each slowed the other down.

nodes.label: HSTU
nodes.idea: Meta treats a user's actions as a sequence and trains a generative model to predict what comes next.
nodes.impact: Quality scaled with compute like an LLM's, and LinkedIn later rebuilt its feed ranking the same way.

from.why: Feature-heavy DLRMs stopped improving with more compute, unlike language models.

nodes.label: Wide EP
nodes.idea: With wide expert parallelism, DeepSeek spreads each layer's experts over many nodes so each sees a large batch.
nodes.impact: SGLang and vLLM rebuilt it in the open for serving large mixture-of-experts models.

from.why: Mixture-of-experts models gave each expert too few tokens per GPU, even with the phases split.

main.title: CMU 10-414/714: Deep Learning Systems
main.why: Automatic differentiation, layers, optimizers and GPU operations, each built from scratch into a small deep learning library. In English.

main.title: PyTorch 2: Faster Machine Learning Through Dynamic Python Bytecode Transformation and Graph Compilation
main.why: Eager PyTorch is flexible but hard to compile, so TorchDynamo captures graphs from ordinary Python bytecode and TorchInductor compiles them to Triton and C++.

background.title: PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library

main.title: Introducing Triton: Open-source GPU programming for neural networks
main.why: Fast CUDA kernels need expert tuning, so Triton lets you write them in Python over blocks while the compiler handles memory and scheduling.
Attention is bound by GPU memory traffic, so FlashAttention computes it tile by tile in on-chip SRAM.

background.title: Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles

further.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision

main.title: PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training
main.why: Data-parallel training waits on gradient sync, so PyTorch DDP all-reduces gradients in buckets while the backward pass is still running.

main.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
main.why: Data parallelism copies all model state to every GPU, so ZeRO shards optimizer state, gradients and weights across workers.

main.title: The Ultra-Scale Playbook: Training LLMs on GPU Clusters
main.why: Large models need more than data parallelism, and this playbook explains tensor, context, pipeline and expert parallelism and how to combine them.

further.title: MegaScale: Scaling Large Language Model Training to More Than 10,000 GPUs

main.why: KV cache fragmentation capped serving batch sizes, so vLLM's PagedAttention stores the cache in fixed-size blocks like OS pages.

background.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models

further.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs

main.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
main.why: Each generated token needs a full pass of the large model, so a small model drafts tokens and the large model verifies them together, with unchanged output.

main.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
main.why: Large models are too big to serve cheaply, so GPTQ quantizes their weights to a few bits after training using second-order error correction.

main.title: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving
main.why: Prefill and decoding interfere when batched together, so DistServe runs them on separate GPUs, each with its own parallelism.

further.title: Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve

main.why: Scoring every video per request is impossible, so YouTube splits recommendation into a candidate generation network and a ranking network.
Recommendation models are dominated by huge embedding tables, so DLRM shards them with model parallelism and replicates the MLPs with data parallelism.
Aggregated features lose the order and detail of user events, so Meta's ads models embed each event and pool the sequence with attention.
Feature-heavy recommenders stop improving with more compute, so HSTU recasts recommendation as generative sequence transduction that scales like an LLM.

further.why: LinkedIn replaced its many retrieval sources with one LLM dual encoder, and its per-post CPU ranking with a sequence transformer on GPUs.

main.why: Sequence recommenders at LLM scale waste GPUs on padding and exposed communication, so GEM training uses jagged attention and topology-aware parallelism.

main.title: Embedding-based Retrieval in Facebook Search
main.why: Term matching misses semantically related results, so Facebook Search adds embedding retrieval and serves ANN inside its existing inverted index.

further.why: LinkedIn rebuilt search around LLMs, which parse each query, retrieve by exact kNN over embeddings on GPUs and rank with a small distilled model.

main.title: The Faiss library
main.why: Vector search trades accuracy, speed and memory, and the Faiss paper maps that space through compression codecs, inverted-file indexes and graph indexes.
